_description: Literature heat fluxes (W) and event-plume heat contents (J) for placing the NESCA megaplume on a ladder of scales, from a single black smoker to the heat loss of the whole Earth. Every value was read in the source text quoted here; superscripts are written as ^. Entries carry low_W/high_W for fluxes and energy_J/low_J/high_J for heat contents. ladder_rung: 1 smoker, 2 vent field, 3 ridge segment, 4 megaplume or event plume, 5 global ridge axis, 6 global hydrothermal, 7 ocean floor, 8 whole Earth. 'recommended' marks the core set for the ladder figure or sentence.

entries.quantity: Heat output of a single black-smoker chimney (Juan de Fuca Ridge, orifice velocity-temperature measurements)
entries.value_note: value_W is the Endeavour-field average per smoker; low/high are the full range over individual smokers. The Cleft-field average is 3.1 MW.
entries.quote: Values for individual smokers vary from 0.1 to 94 MW, with an average of 6.2 MW at the Endeavour field and 3.1 MW at the Cleft field.
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, Crossref metadata (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/93JB02800); identical text in OpenAlex

entries.quantity: Heat output of the black smokers of the Main Endeavour vent field (smokers only; diffuse flow excluded)
entries.value_note: 364 +/- 73 MW. Same paper: smokers carry only 4-14% of the total advective heat flux of these vent fields, so the whole-field output is larger.
entries.quote: The estimated power output from smokers alone is 49±13 MW for the Plume site, Vent 1 and Vent 3 on the southern Cleft segment near 45°N; 364±73 MW for the main vent field on the Endeavour Segment near 48°N; and 122±61 MW for the Tubeworm field 2 km north.
entries.quote_2: These values constitute only 4% to 14% of the total advective heat flux estimated for these vent fields from measurements in the nonbuoyant plume and of diffuse flow at the seafloor, indicating that most of the heat advected at these hydrothermal vent sites is carried by diffuse rather than focused flow.

entries.quantity: Total heat output of the TAG hydrothermal field, Mid-Atlantic Ridge 26 N (focused plus diffuse)
entries.value_note: Range as published (500-900 MW); no central value given. Diffuse flow is 3/4 to 6/7 of it.
entries.quote: the total heat flux of 500–900 MW for the TAG vent field
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, Crossref metadata (api.crossref.org/works/10.1144/GSL.SP.1993.076.01.14). The surrounding sentence carries a Crossref typesetting duplication ('about ¾ to 3/4 to 6/7 of'), so only the clean clause is quoted.

entries.quantity: Total heat output of the Lucky Strike hydrothermal field, Mid-Atlantic Ridge (focused plus diffuse)
entries.value_note: Range as published (~200-1000 MW); 75% to >90% carried by diffuse outflow.
entries.quote: The coupling of mosaic interpretation and available field measurements allow us to independently estimate the heat flux of the Lucky Strike system at ∼200 to 1000 MW, with 75% to >90% of this flux taken up by diffuse hydrothermal outflow.
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, Crossref metadata (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/2011GC003990); identical in OpenAlex

entries.quantity: Hydrothermal heat flux of the southern Juan de Fuca Ridge segment (continuous venting plus episodic megaplumes, late 1980s)
entries.quote: The flux of hydrothermal heat from continuous venting and episodic megaplumes on the southern Juan de Fuca Ridge is presently 4 − 10 × 10^9 W, a factor of 5–10 greater than various geophysical model calculations for this ridge segment.
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, OpenAlex (api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.1029/JB094iB07p09237) and NOAA/PMEL full-text reproduction https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/pubs/outstand/bake1050/abstract.shtml

entries.quantity: Source heat flux needed to form the 1986 Juan de Fuca megaplume (megaplume 1, EP86) for a 2-20 day discharge
entries.value_note: 7e11 W for a 2-day discharge, 7e10 W for a 20-day discharge. Abstract: megaplume heat and volume fluxes are 10^2-10^3 greater than ordinary vent fields.
entries.quote: Using the bounds of 2–20 days cited above, the mass and heat fluxes necessary to form megaplume 1 would have ranged from 30–3 × 10^7 g/s (at 350°C) and 70–7 × 10^10 W, respectively.
entries.quote_2: The extraordinary heat and volume fluxes associated with megaplumes (10^2 − 10^3 greater than ordinary vent fields), as well as their typical hydrothermal chemistry, suggest that they resulted from tectonic or hydraulic fracturing that suddenly increased the permeability of the hydrothermal fluid reservoir in the axial crust.
entries.source_of_quote: Discussion section, NOAA/PMEL full-text reproduction of the published paper, https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/pubs/outstand/bake1050/discuss.shtml (quote_2: Abstract, same site and OpenAlex)

entries.quantity: Heat content of the 1986 Juan de Fuca megaplume (megaplume 1, EP86)
entries.value_note: energy_J is the field-integrated excess heat Q_t; high_J is the model total heat released including the entrainment correction. The abstract gives the generic range 10^16-10^17 J for megaplume-forming fluids.
entries.quote: For megaplume 1, Qt is estimated to be 6.7 × 10^16 J, and Hv is estimated to be 3.5 × 10^8 J m−1 s−1 as described earlier.
entries.quote_2: Using a value of 4000 m d for ℓτ, the total volume and heat released during the megaplume 1 event were 7.6 × 10^7 m3 and 1.2 × 10^17 J, respectively.
entries.quote_3: A plume model that relates the heat flux to the observed plume rise height of ∼1000 m finds that the total heat content of the fluids that formed the megaplumes was 10^16–10^17 J, or equivalently a fluid volume of 3–8 × 10^7 m3 at 350°C.
entries.source_of_quote: Plume Model section, NOAA/PMEL full-text reproduction https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/pubs/outstand/bake1050/plume.shtml; quote_3 from the Abstract (OpenAlex and PMEL)

entries.quantity: Heat content of the 1987 Juan de Fuca megaplume (megaplume 2, EP87)
entries.duration: not constrained separately; lens shape implies a short-duration venting episode
entries.value_note: energy_J is the field-integrated excess heat; high_J is the model total for a megaplume-2-sized event.
entries.quote: The ΔT at the core of megaplume 2 was 0.23°C and the total excess heat (1) where ρ is density, Cp is specific heat, and t and Vi are the mean temperature anomaly and the volume between each ΔT contour (Figure 3), respectively, was 3.2 × 10^16 J, or again about 50% of the excess contained in megaplume 1.
entries.quote_2: The comparative source strength for a megaplume 2-sized event is 1900 m d with a total volume and heat content of 3.6 × 10^7 m3 and 5.8 × 10^16 J, respectively.
entries.source_of_quote: Results and Plume Model sections, NOAA/PMEL full-text reproduction https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/pubs/outstand/bake1050/results.shtml and plume.shtml (the HTML interleaves equation (1) into the sentence)

entries.quantity: Energy equivalence of the 1986 megaplume: formed in a few days, equal to the annual output of 200-2000 high-temperature chimneys
entries.value_note: Qualitative comparison; no watt value given in the abstract. Useful as a framing sentence.
entries.quote: The megaplume was formed in a few days yet equalled the annual output of between 200 and 2,000 high-temperature chimneys.

entries.quantity: Excess heat of the three event plumes of the 1993 CoAxial eruption, Juan de Fuca Ridge
entries.duration: plumes released intermittently with seismic pulses between 28 June and 14 July 1993; per-plume durations not given in the abstract
entries.value_note: Plume volumes 1.3-4 x 10^10 m3. These are smaller than EP86/EP87.
entries.quote: Between July 3 and 26 we detected at least three event plumes ranging in plume volume from 1.3 to 4 × 10^10 m³, and in excess heat from 2.2 to 12.4 × 10^15 J.

entries.quantity: Excess heat of the unusually large event plume above the slow-spreading Carlsberg Ridge, NW Indian Ocean
entries.value_note: Published as an upper value ('up to 24 x 10^16 J'); plume 70 km long and up to 4540 km3 in volume. Larger than the 2e17 J upper end of the Pegler & Ferguson (2021) estimate for NESCA.
entries.quote: At 70 km long, up to 4540 km^3 in volume and with up to 24 × 10^16 J of excess heat, this event plume was substantially larger than previous ones and demonstrates that dispersion of hydrothermal heat and biological products from slow spreading ridges may be more significant and effective than hitherto imagined.
entries.quote_2: Each plume often contains as much hydrothermal effluent and heat as chronic hydrothermal venting from a typical vent site discharges during a year.
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, Crossref metadata (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/2006GL026048); article number L10608 confirmed from the NOAA/PMEL publication list of E. T. Baker

entries.quantity: Global mid-ocean-ridge axial hydrothermal heat flux
entries.value_note: Range as published (2-4 TW); includes both black-smoker and diffuse axial flow.
entries.quote: Geophysical estimates of mid-ocean ridge axial heat fluxes (2–4 × 10^12 W) and of the total hydrothermal flux (9 ± 2 × 10^12 W) are well established.
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, Crossref metadata (api.crossref.org/works/10.1146/annurev.earth.24.1.191); identical in OpenAlex

entries.quantity: Global hydrothermal heat flux through the ocean crust (axis plus flanks)
entries.quote: Geophysical estimates of mid-ocean ridge axial heat fluxes (2–4 × 10^12 W) and of the total hydrothermal flux (9 ± 2 × 10^12 W) are well established.

entries.quantity: Global hydrothermal heat flux through the oceanic lithosphere (upper bound), and the predicted total oceanic heat flux
entries.value_note: 11 TW = 34% of the predicted 32 TW oceanic heat flux (GDH1 model). The authors state these are upper bounds; about 30% of the hydrothermal flux is in crust younger than 1 Ma. The abstract gives no +/- uncertainty; the '11 +/- 4 TW' often attributed to this paper was not read and is not used.
entries.quote: We estimate that of the predicted global oceanic heat flux of 32×10^12 W, 34% (11×10^12 W) occurs by hydrothermal flow. Approximately 30% of the hydrothermal heat flux occurs in crust younger than 1 Ma, so the majority of this flux is off‐ridge. These hydrothermal heat flux estimates are upper bounds, because heat flow measurements require sediment at the site and so are made preferentially at topographic lows, where heat flow may be depressed.
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract, Crossref metadata (api.crossref.org/works/10.1029/93JB02222); identical in OpenAlex

entries.quantity: Total heat loss through the ocean floor
entries.value_note: Table 7 of the paper: ocean area 3.028e14 m2, 31.9 TW, mean 105.4 mW m-2. No separate uncertainty for the oceanic part in Table 7; the global total carries +/-2 TW (2 sigma).
entries.quote: Table 7. Summary of continental and oceanic heat flow from our preferred estimates. [...] Ocean 3.028 × 10^14 [m2] 31.9 [TW] 105.4 [mW m−2]
entries.source_of_quote: Table 7, open-access full text PDF https://se.copernicus.org/articles/1/5/2010/se-1-5-2010.pdf (table row transcribed; column units in brackets)

entries.quantity: Total surface heat loss of the Earth
entries.value_note: 47 +/- 2 TW; the text states the error is 2 standard deviations (46.7 TW rounded).
entries.quote: Our final preferred estimate is 47±2 TW, which is greater than previous estimates.
entries.quote_2: Our final preferred value is 46.7 TW, with an error of 2 TW (2 standard deviations).
entries.source_of_quote: Abstract (Crossref metadata) and Section 3 of the open-access full text https://se.copernicus.org/articles/1/5/2010/se-1-5-2010.pdf

entries.quantity: Total surface heat loss of the Earth (earlier estimate)
entries.value_note: Mean oceanic heat flow 101 mW m-2, continental 65 mW m-2. The abstract gives no uncertainty ('44.2 TW +/- 1 TW' appears only as quoted by Davies and Davies 2010, so it is not used here).
entries.quote: The mean heat flows of continents and oceans are 65 and 101 mW m−2, respectively, which when areally weighted yield a global mean of 87 mW m−2 and a global heat loss of 44.2 × 10^12 W, an increase of some 4–8% over earlier estimates.
